raw_case_text:
A 62-year-old male patient was admitted in February 2025 due to an elevated CA19-9 level, which had been consistently high for the past year. He first visited a local hospital a year ago when he presented with a cough, at which time an elevated CA19-9 level of 518 U/ml was detected; however, he did not regard this as significant at that time. Two months prior to his admission, a routine health check revealed a substantial increase in his CA19-9 level to 1303.79 U/ml, which further rose to 1524.93 U/ml 1 month later. Despite these alarming results, the patient reported no significant discomfort. Consequently, he was referred to our department for further evaluation of the elevated CA19-9 level. His medical history was unremarkable, with no chronic illnesses and no history of smoking or alcohol consumption. Upon examination, his vital signs were stable; but, he appeared slightly underweight. Respiratory assessment revealed coarse breath sounds in the left lung, while breath sounds in the right lung were clear. Cardiac and abdominal examinations showed no abnormalities. Routine laboratory tests - including a complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and biochemical profile - returned normal results. A chest CT scan indicated pulmonary sequestration in the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe, with signs suggestive of infection. Additionally, a few enlarged lymph nodes were noted in the retroperitoneum. An abdominal enhanced CT scan revealed a hypervascular nodule in the retroperitoneum; follow-up imaging was recommended by the clinical team if deemed necessary. Furthermore, there was a lobulated mass in the left lower lobe with local calcification, exhibiting uneven enhancement and associated with the descending aorta, raising suspicion for pulmonary sequestration. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pancreaticobiliary system showed no abnormalities. However, an enhanced MRI of the pancreas indicated a nodule in the tail of the pancreas, accompanied by signal abnormalities in the body and tail, suggesting a high likelihood of a benign process, potentially due to inflammation, along with a few enlarged retroperitoneal lymph nodes. An endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration biopsy identified a hypoechoic mass in the tail of the pancreas and involvement of the retroperitoneal lymph nodes. The pathological examination of the biopsy revealed significant necrosis and inflammatory cells in the pancreas, while cytology from the retroperitoneal lymph node showed an abundance of lymphocytes. A PET-CT scan demonstrated a mass in the left lower lung with punctate calcifications and unevenly increased glucose metabolism, consistent with previous CT findings that suggested pulmonary sequestration.
Additionally, multiple inflammatory foci were observed in both lungs, with increased metabolic activity in the hilar lymph nodes - indicative of reactive lymphoid hyperplasia, alongside calcification of the aortic wall. The scan also revealed multiple nodules in the retroperitoneal area with increased metabolic activity, raising concerns for reactive lymphoid hyperplasia of the lymph nodes; however, other conditions could not be excluded, prompting a recommendation for a follow-up CT scan. After consultations with the respiratory and thoracic surgery departments, surgical intervention was advised. A preoperative enhanced chest CT indicated a lobulated mass in the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe, measuring 75 x 51 mm, consistent with pulmonary sequestration, with visible vascular supply from the descending aorta (Fig. 1A-C).The patient underwent a lobectomy in February 2025 (Fig. 1D). By postoperative day 2, their CA19-9 levels had decreased significantly. Pathological examination revealed widened interlobular septa, fibrosis, irregular thick-walled vessels, chronic lymphocytic inflammation accompanied by mucus, bronchial hyperplasia, and fungal hyphae indicative of Aspergillus infection. Immunohistochemical staining for CA19-9 showed a positive expression of CA19-9. The resection margins were negative for tumor involvement. Subsequently, CA19-9 levels normalized by 3 months after surgery (Fig. 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 62-year-old asymptomatic male presented with a 1-year history of persistently and progressively elevated serum CA19-9 levels.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One year prior to admission in February 2025, the patient visited a local hospital for a cough and was found to have an elevated serum CA19-9 level of 518 U/mL. Although his cough resolved and he felt completely well, routine health checks 2 months and 1 month prior to admission showed a marked rise in serum CA19-9 to 1,303.79 U/mL and 1,524.93 U/mL, respectively, prompting referral for malignancy workup.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history; no chronic illnesses; non-smoker and non-drinker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for current cough, fever, chest pain, abdominal pain, or weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs were stable; patient appeared slightly underweight. Lung auscultation revealed coarse breath sounds over the left lung and clear breath sounds on the right; cardiac and abdominal examinations were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum CA19-9 was markedly elevated at 518 U/mL (1 year prior), 1,303.79 U/mL (2 months prior), and 1,524.93 U/mL (1 month prior to admission). Routine CBC, ESR, and serum biochemistry profile were completely normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a 75 x 51 mm lobulated mass with focal punctate calcifications and heterogeneous enhancement in the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe supplied by an anomalous systemic artery arising from the descending thoracic aorta, diagnostic of pulmonary sequestration. Abdominal CT, pancreaticobiliary MRI, PET-CT, and endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (EUS-FNA) of a pancreatic tail nodule and retroperitoneal lymph nodes showed only benign pancreatic necrosis/inflammation and reactive lymphoid hyperplasia without malignancy. Following left lower lobectomy in February 2025, histopathology of the resected sequestered lung revealed widened fibrotic interlobular septa, thick-walled aberrant vessels, bronchial hyperplasia, chronic lymphocytic inflammation with mucus impaction, strong CA19-9 immunohistochemical positivity in the bronchial epithelium, and intraluminal fungal hyphae characteristic of Aspergillus infection, with tumor-free margins.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Left lower lobe intralobar pulmonary sequestration complicated by localized Aspergillus infection causing marked benign elevation of serum CA19-9 (1,524.93 U/mL), definitively confirmed by contrast-enhanced CT angiography, EUS-FNA ruling out pancreaticobiliary malignancy, and lobectomy histopathology demonstrating Aspergillus hyphae and strong CA19-9 immunostaining within the sequestered lung tissue. Treated with surgical left lower lobectomy in February 2025, resulting in an immediate drop in serum CA19-9 by postoperative day 2 and complete normalization of CA19-9 levels at 3 months post-surgery.
